title: Partitions and segments on disk: retention and compaction
goal: By the end, you can explain why a Kafka topic is split into partitions and each partition into files called segments, predict what retention will delete (whole segments, never single records), say what compaction keeps, and explain how old segments can move off the broker's disk.
opening:
Picture a café that writes every order in a notebook. When a notebook fills, the owner shelves it and starts a new one. Her rule is to keep orders for a week, so each Monday she throws out every notebook whose last order is over a week old.

One Monday, an inspector finds a twelve-day-old order on the shelf. The owner didn't break her rule: that notebook also holds orders from last Thursday, and she only throws out whole notebooks.

It's easy to read "keep for 7 days" as "gone at 7 days": that's what the setting says. But Kafka, the program that keeps logs of records for other programs to read, cleans up like the owner.

The log: Kafka's one big idea built one growing log and left two questions: how do many readers share it, and what stops it filling the disk? In this lesson, we'll split a topic into partitions and files, then watch retention delete whole files and compaction keep each key's last value. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A Kafka topic is set to keep records for one hour. Kafka stores the records in files, and one file holds records 208 to 311. Records 208 to 249 were written two hours ago, and 250 to 311 a minute ago. After the next clean-up, what can a reader still read from that file?
options: Records 250 to 311: Kafka deletes each record once it's older than an hour
Records 208 to 311: the file stays whole until its newest record is older than an hour
Nothing: one expired record makes the whole file expire
Records 208 to 249 only: the clean-up removes the newest records first
warmup.why: Kafka deletes whole files, and a file expires only when its newest record is older than the limit. Records 208 to 249 are past the hour, but they share a file with fresh records, so they stay readable, like the old orders in the café's notebook. The first option is the record-by-record picture most people start with. The lab's broker test shows a real broker keeping exactly these records.

sections.h: One log is too slow for one reader: a topic is split into partitions
sections.body:
The last lesson built one log, a file you only add to, where the broker numbers every record with an offset and each reader keeps one number, its position. One log for a whole topic runs into two limits, though.

The first limit is the reader. A consumer group, a set of consumers that read a topic as one, keeps one position per log. Two members of the same group can't share one position: they would both read offset 50, or one would skip records the other hasn't finished. So inside a group, only one consumer reads a given log at a time. In numbers: if the fraud check needs 2 ms per payment, one consumer handles at most 500 payments a second. At a peak of 3,000 payments a second, it falls 2,500 records further behind every second.

The second limit is the machine. One log is one set of files on one broker's disk, so one broker takes every write for the topic.

Kafka's fix is to split a topic into several logs, called **partitions**. Each partition is a complete log of its own, exactly like the last lesson's: offsets start at 0, and every group has its own position in it. With 6 partitions, six fraud-check consumers in one group each read one partition, and together they handle 6 × 500 = 3,000 payments a second. Different partitions can also live on different brokers, as the next lesson shows.

The split breaks something. One log had one order for everything. Six logs don't: offset 10 in partition 0 and offset 10 in partition 3 have no order between them. For payments that matters, because the capture of a payment (when the money moves) must not be handled before its authorization (when the bank set the money aside).

The fix is the record's **key**, the part that says what the record is about, such as an account or a card. The producer runs the key through a hash function, a calculation that turns any key into a number and always gives the same number for the same key. That number picks a partition. So every record with the same key lands in the same partition and stays in order there. Key payments by account, and all of one account's records keep their order, while different accounts spread across partitions. (Splitting data: key ranges, hashes and tenants, in the Partitioning track, used the same idea for databases.) Records without a key are spread across partitions in batches, groups of records sent together; lesson 5 of this track has the details.

**Order is kept only within a partition. Give records that must stay in order the same key.**

On the broker's disk, each partition is a directory named after the topic and the partition number: `card-auths-0`, `card-auths-1`, `card-auths-2`. Everything about the partition lives in its directory, and nothing in it refers to another partition.

Choose the number of partitions with care. You can add partitions later but never remove them, and adding them changes which partition a key maps to. An account's records written before the change stay in one partition, later ones may land in another, and a consumer can then see them out of order. For a payments topic keyed by account, decide the count at the start.

Each of those directories holds a log that grows all day. Next, we'll look inside one.

try.title: Three partitions, three logs
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the broker with `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait`. (Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers; this starts one Kafka broker in one.) Then open a shell, a command prompt, inside it: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka bash`.
Run the commands below. They create a topic with 3 partitions, add six card authorizations with keys, and read them back with each record's partition and offset.
Predict before you run: will six records with three keys land two per partition?
Keep the shell open for the next Try its.

code.title: inside the kafka container
code.src:
cd /opt/kafka/bin
B=localhost:9092
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $B --create --topic card-auths --partitions 3

printf 'card-1:auth 10.00\ncard-2:auth 25.00\ncard-3:auth 7.50\ncard-1:auth 3.20\ncard-2:auth 99.00\ncard-1:auth 1.00\n' \
  | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-auths \
      --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=:

./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-auths --from-beginning --max-messages 6 \
  --formatter-property print.partition=true --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.key=true

ls -d /var/lib/kafka/data/card-auths-*

try.expect:
```text
Partition:2	Offset:0	card-1	auth 10.00
Partition:2	Offset:1	card-1	auth 3.20
Partition:2	Offset:2	card-1	auth 1.00
Partition:1	Offset:0	card-2	auth 25.00
Partition:1	Offset:1	card-3	auth 7.50
Partition:1	Offset:2	card-2	auth 99.00
/var/lib/kafka/data/card-auths-0
/var/lib/kafka/data/card-auths-1
/var/lib/kafka/data/card-auths-2
```
All three card-1 records are in partition 2, in the order you wrote them. card-2 and card-3 both hash to partition 1, and partition 0 got nothing: keys are hashed, not dealt out in turn. Each partition counts its own offsets from 0. The hash always gives the same answer, so you'll get the same partitions, but the two partitions may print in the other order. (The KIP-848 notice from the last lesson prints too; it's left out here.)

sections.h: A partition is a chain of files called segments
sections.body:
A log only grows. Do the sums: at 3,000 payments a second of about 1 KB each, a topic takes about 3 MB a second. That's about 260 GB a day, and about 1.8 TB a week. Sooner or later, the broker must delete the oldest records.

The simplest design keeps each partition in one big file and deletes from the front. That doesn't work, because a file system, the part of the operating system that keeps files on disk, can cheaply cut a file short at its end but not at its start. To drop the oldest 260 GB from a 1.8 TB file, the broker would have to copy the remaining 1.5 TB into a new file, every day.

So the broker cuts the log into a chain of files called **segments**, like the café's notebooks. Only the newest one, the **active segment**, takes new records. When the active segment is full, the broker closes it and opens a new one; that's called **rolling** the segment. A closed segment never changes again. Deleting old data now means deleting old files, which costs almost nothing however big they are.

Each segment is named after its **base offset**, the offset of its first record, padded with zeros to 20 digits. The segment that starts at offset 208 is the file `00000000000000000208.log`. The names solve the next problem, finding a record. To read offset 230, the broker looks for the segment with the largest base offset at or below 230. That's `...208.log`. The broker keeps its list of segments sorted by base offset, so the lookup is quick.

Inside that file there's a second problem. A segment can be 1 GiB, and reading it from the start at, say, 2 GB a second would take half a second for one lookup. So next to each `.log` file sits an `.index` file that maps offsets to byte positions in the `.log` file, like the index at the back of a book. It's **sparse**: the broker adds an entry about every 4,096 bytes of data (`index.interval.bytes`), not one per record, which keeps the index small enough to hold in memory. The broker looks up 230 in the index, gets the byte position of the nearest entry at or below it, and reads forward a few kilobytes to offset 230. A third file, `.timeindex`, maps times to offsets in the same sparse way, so a consumer can ask for the first record after nine o'clock.

Two topic settings decide when the active segment rolls. (GiB and MiB count in powers of two: 1 MiB is 1,048,576 bytes, a little more than 1 MB.)

| Setting | Default | The segment rolls when |
|---|---|---|
| `segment.bytes` | 1 GiB | the next batch would make the file bigger than this |
| `segment.ms` | 7 days | the segment is older than this when a new record arrives |

Kafka 4.0 raised the smallest allowed `segment.bytes` to 1 MiB. To see many segments in a lab, you write large records into 1 MiB segments, which the Try it below does.

Segments make deleting cheap. Next, we'll see which ones go, and why an old record can outlive its limit.

try.title: Watch segments roll
steps: In the container shell, create a topic with one partition and the smallest segment size Kafka 4.4 accepts, 1 MiB.
Write 400 records of 10,000 bytes each, about 4 MB in all, with `kafka-producer-perf-test.sh`, a tool that comes with Kafka for timing producers.
Predict how many `.log` files you'll see and roughly where each one starts. Then list them and print the earliest and latest offsets.

code.title: inside the kafka container, in /opt/kafka/bin
code.src:
B=localhost:9092
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $B --create --topic ledger --partitions 1 --config segment.bytes=1048576

./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic ledger --num-records 400 --record-size 10000 --throughput -1 \
  --command-property bootstrap.servers=$B

ls -l /var/lib/kafka/data/ledger-0/ | grep '\.log'
./kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic ledger --time earliest
./kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic ledger --time latest

try.expect:
```text
400 records sent, 1126.760563 records/sec (10.75 MB/sec), 96.03 ms avg latency, ...
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser  1047488 Nov  7 17:50 00000000000000000000.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser  1047488 Nov  7 17:50 00000000000000000104.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser  1047488 Nov  7 17:50 00000000000000000208.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser   886336 Nov  7 17:50 00000000000000000312.log
ledger:0:0
ledger:0:400
```
Four segments: three closed ones with 104 records each, and the active one, named 312, with the last 88. Two 10 kB records don't fit in the producer's default batch of 16 KiB, so every record went in a batch of its own, about 10,072 bytes on disk. 104 of those fit in 1 MiB, and the 105th rolled the segment. The perf-test numbers depend on your machine. `kafka-get-offsets.sh` prints `topic:partition:offset`, and the latest offset is the end offset.

sections.h: Retention deletes whole segments, never single records
sections.body:
Retention decides when old data goes. A topic with `cleanup.policy=delete`, the default, has two limits. `retention.ms` (7 days by default) caps the age of the data, and `retention.bytes` (-1 by default, meaning no limit) caps the size of each partition.

Because the broker deletes files, not records, it needs a rule for a whole file. A segment may go only when every record in it may go. The newest record in a segment is always the last one to expire, so the rule is: a segment has expired when its **newest** record is older than `retention.ms`. That's the café owner's rule for her notebooks. Every `log.retention.check.interval.ms` (5 minutes by default; the lab broker uses 5 seconds), the broker walks each partition's segments from the oldest. It deletes each expired one whole, and stops at the first segment that hasn't expired. For size, it deletes the oldest segments as long as the partition would still hold at least `retention.bytes` without them.

The rule has three results that surprise people.

Records live longer than `retention.ms` says. An old record shares its segment with newer ones and goes only when the newest has expired. On a quiet topic, a 1 GiB segment may take days to fill, so it rolls on `segment.ms` after 7 days, and then waits until its newest record is 7 days old too. Ask for 7 days, and the oldest records can stay for about 14. If you must delete soon after the limit, make segments roll more often, say every 6 hours with `segment.ms`.

The earliest offset jumps. When a segment goes, the partition's **earliest offset**, the oldest offset still readable, moves to the next segment's base offset: 104 records at once in the Try it below, never one at a time. A consumer group whose committed offset (its saved position) now points into deleted data gets an out-of-range error on its next read. The consumer setting `auto.offset.reset` decides what happens next. With its default, `latest`, the consumer jumps to the end of the partition and skips everything in between, with a single line in its log to say so. A consumer that mustn't skip data sets it to `earliest`, to read what's left, or `none`, to stop with an error and let a person decide.

Deleting on disk is lazy. The broker first renames the files to end in `.deleted`, and removes them a minute later (`log.segment.delete.delay.ms`), so that a reader still using a file can finish.

The active segment isn't protected, either. If every record in a partition has expired, the broker rolls a new, empty active segment and then deletes all the old ones. The partition is empty, but its offsets keep counting from where they were.

**Retention keeps records at least as long as you ask, never exactly as long. Check the earliest offset, not the setting.**

Age suits a history of payments. Next, we'll meet a topic where age is the wrong rule.

The size cap removed exactly one segment, because removing the next one as well would have left the partition below 2,500,000 bytes. The earliest offset jumped from 0 to 104 in one step. sections.h: Compaction keeps the last value for each key
sections.body:
Some topics hold a current state rather than a history. Take a `card-status` topic. Every time a card is activated, frozen or closed, a program writes a record whose key is the card's id and whose value is its new status. Other programs read the topic from the beginning when they start, to build a map in memory from each card to its status.

Retention by age is wrong for this topic. A card whose status last changed three weeks ago would drop out after 7 days, and a program rebuilding its map would think the card doesn't exist. Keeping everything forever is wrong too. With 10 million cards and a few updates each a day, the topic grows without end, and a rebuild reads years of history only to keep the last line for each card.

What you want is the last record for each key, like a phone's contact list, which keeps each friend's newest number and forgets the old ones. That's what `cleanup.policy=compact` gives you. Instead of deleting old segments by age, the broker keeps at least the last record for every key, and removes older records that a newer one with the same key has replaced.

A helper that runs in the background on the broker, the **log cleaner**, does the work. It picks the partition with the largest share of not-yet-cleaned ("dirty") data, once that share passes `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio` (0.5 by default, meaning half). It reads the dirty segments and builds a map from each key to the offset of that key's last record. Then it copies the closed segments, keeping only records whose offset is the last one for their key, and swaps the copies in.

Three rules matter to anyone who reads a compacted topic. Offsets never change: survivors keep their original offsets, so a compacted partition has gaps, and consumers skip them without noticing. Order never changes either. And the cleaner never touches the active segment, so the newest records look like a plain log until their segment rolls.

How do you delete a card, when you can only add records? You add a record with the card's key and a null value, called a **tombstone**:

```java
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("card-status", "card-2", null));   // tombstone: card-2 is gone
```

```kotlin
producer.send(ProducerRecord<String, String>("card-status", "card-2", null))   // tombstone: card-2 is gone
```

Kotlin needs the types written out, `<String, String>`, because it can't tell the value's type from `null` alone.

Compaction then removes the older values for card-2. It keeps the tombstone itself for `delete.retention.ms` (1 day by default), because a consumer that never sees the tombstone would keep card-2 in its map forever. The clock starts when the cleaner first reaches the tombstone; `kafka-dump-log.sh` shows the end of that window as `deleteHorizonMs`. A consumer that falls more than a day behind can still miss it.

Compaction doesn't stop repeats from reaching consumers. It keeps the last value per key only in closed segments, and only once the cleaner gets there. Until then, every old value is still in the log and consumers read them all, so your code must handle every record. You can also combine both policies: `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` keeps the last value per key and also deletes segments past retention.

All of this still happens on the broker's own disk. Next, we'll ask whether old segments have to stay there at all.

try.title: Compact a card-status topic
steps: In the container shell, create a compacted topic whose segments roll after 5 seconds, with a low dirty ratio so the cleaner starts right away.
Write six status updates that end with a tombstone for card-2. The `null.marker` setting turns the text `NULL` into a null value.
The script then waits, writes one more record to roll the first segment, and waits again so the cleaner can run. Predict which offsets survive before you read the output.
Exit the shell and stop the broker from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml down -v`.

code.title: inside the kafka container, in /opt/kafka/bin
code.src:
B=localhost:9092
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $B --create --topic card-status \
  --config cleanup.policy=compact --config segment.ms=5000 --config min.cleanable.dirty.ratio=0.01

printf 'card-1:active\ncard-2:active\ncard-1:frozen\ncard-3:active\ncard-1:active\ncard-2:NULL\n' \
  | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-status \
      --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=: --reader-property null.marker=NULL
sleep 6
# one more record: it rolls the first segment, which can now be compacted
printf 'card-4:active\n' | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-status \
  --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=:
sleep 6

./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server $B --topic card-status --from-beginning --max-messages 4 \
  --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.key=true
./kafka-dump-log.sh --files /var/lib/kafka/data/card-status-0/00000000000000000000.log --print-data-log

try.expect:
```text
Offset:3	card-3	active
Offset:4	card-1	active
Offset:5	card-2	null
Offset:6	card-4	active
```
and from the dump (trimmed):
```text
baseOffset: 0 lastOffset: 5 count: 3 ... deleteHorizonMs: OptionalLong[1794160261750] ...
| offset: 3 ... key: card-3 payload: active
| offset: 4 ... key: card-1 payload: active
| offset: 5 ... keySize: 6 valueSize: -1 ... key: card-2
```
Offsets 0, 1 and 2 are gone: a later record with the same key replaced each one. The survivors kept their offsets, so the partition now starts with a gap at 0 to 2. The tombstone for card-2 is still there (`valueSize: -1`), and its `deleteHorizonMs` is one day after the cleaner first reached it. Offset 6 is in the active segment, which the cleaner never touches. If you still see all six old records, the cleaner hasn't run yet: wait a few seconds and read again.

sections.h: Moving old segments off the broker: tiered storage and diskless topics
sections.body:
A closed segment never changes, so it doesn't have to stay on the broker that wrote it. That lets Kafka keep storage apart from the machines that do the work, the idea from Growing past one machine: shared-nothing, shared-disk and the cloud. Keep the lasting copy in object storage, and treat the broker's disk as a cache. **Object storage** is a cloud service, such as Amazon S3, that keeps files cheaply and safely; you rent space by the gigabyte and read files over the network.

Start with what keeping everything on the broker costs. The topic from the second section takes 3 MB a second, about 1.8 TB a week. The next lesson keeps every partition on three brokers, so that's 5.4 TB of broker disk for each week kept. Say the rules ask for 13 months. The brokers now need about 300 TB, and adding a broker means copying partitions to it for hours. Yet almost every read is near the end of the log. The old segments sit there for the rare replay.

**Tiered storage** moves them out. It was planned as KIP-405 (a KIP, or Kafka Improvement Proposal, is a written plan for a change to Kafka), and it has been ready for real use since Kafka 3.9. With `remote.storage.enable=true` on a topic, the broker copies each closed segment to remote storage, usually an object store, through a plugin, code you add to the broker, called a `RemoteStorageManager`. It keeps only recent segments on its own disk; `local.retention.ms` and `local.retention.bytes` say how many. Their default, -2, means "the same as `retention.ms` and `retention.bytes`", so nothing leaves until you lower them. `retention.ms` still decides when a record is gone everywhere. A consumer that reads an old offset gets it from the object store without knowing, only more slowly. The active segment always stays local.

Tiered storage leaves writing alone, and in the cloud, writing is where the money goes. Every byte a producer sends is still copied from the broker that takes the partition's writes to two others. A cloud region is split into availability zones, separate data centres a few kilometres apart, and with the three copies in three zones, most copying crosses zones. AWS, Amazon's cloud, charges about $0.02 for every GiB that crosses zones. At 100 MB a second, copying alone moves about 16,000 GiB a day between zones: around $320 a day.

**Diskless topics** (KIP-1150) would remove that traffic. Producers' batches would go straight to object storage, a separate coordinator would give out their offsets, and brokers would keep only bookkeeping, staging space and a cache on their disks. The object store already keeps its own copies, so brokers would stop copying data to each other. The price is time: a write counts once the object store has it. Products that speak Kafka's protocol and already work this way quote write times of roughly 100 to 500 ms, instead of a few milliseconds. Among them are WarpStream (bought by Confluent, a company built around Kafka, in 2024), Redpanda's Cloud Topics (ready for general use in Redpanda 26.1) and AutoMQ. KIP-1150 was accepted in March 2026 but hasn't shipped. Its core designs (KIP-1163 and KIP-1164) were still under discussion in August 2026, and Kafka 4.4 has no diskless setting.

So ask the question from Growing past one machine: where is the lasting copy? On a classic topic, on the brokers' own disks. With tiered storage, recent segments on those disks and older ones in the object store. On a diskless topic, in the object store, with broker disks as a cache.

compare.title: The cleaner's offset map in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin

compare.note: `associate` builds the map in one call and keeps the last value it sees for each key, which is exactly the cleaner's rule. Java's `Collectors.toMap` would throw on the first repeated key unless you pass a merge function such as `(a, b) -> b`, so the plain loop is clearer. Watch the comparison in Java: `==` between two `Long` objects (numbers wrapped in objects) asks whether they are the same object, which happens to work for values up to 127 and fails above. Here `getOffset()` returns a plain `long`, so Java unwraps the other side and compares values. Kotlin's `==` always compares values.

worked.title: Work out what a retention change will delete before you make it

steps.say: The team wants the `settlement-events` topic, the nightly payouts to shops, kept for 3 days instead of 7. Before you change `retention.ms`, find out how much would go. Start with where partition 0 begins today. (`admin` is an `Admin` client, the Kafka library's object for managing topics; repeat for each partition.)
steps.alt_code:
// 1. where partition 0 starts today
val tp = TopicPartition("settlement-events", 0)
val earliest = admin.listOffsets(mapOf(tp to OffsetSpec.earliest()))
    .partitionResult(tp).get().offset()

steps.say: Find the first record younger than 3 days. `OffsetSpec.forTimestamp` asks the broker's time index for the earliest offset whose time is at or after the one you give. If every record is older, it returns -1: everything would go.
steps.alt_code:
// 2. the first record younger than 3 days
val cutoff = System.currentTimeMillis() - Duration.ofDays(3).toMillis()
val firstYoung = admin.listOffsets(mapOf(tp to OffsetSpec.forTimestamp(cutoff)))
    .partitionResult(tp).get().offset()

steps.say: Now apply the segment rule. The broker deletes only whole segments whose newest record is older than the cutoff, so the new earliest offset will be the base offset of the segment that holds `firstYoung`: at or below it, never above. `firstYoung - earliest` is the most that can go; the real number is rounded down to whole segments.
steps.code:
// 3. an upper bound, rounded down to whole segments in practice
System.out.printf("partition 0: up to %,d records older than 3 days%n", firstYoung - earliest);
steps.alt_code:
// 3. an upper bound, rounded down to whole segments in practice
println("partition 0: up to %,d records older than 3 days".format(firstYoung - earliest))

steps.say: Change only the one setting, with `incrementalAlterConfigs`. Then watch the earliest offset over the next retention checks (every 5 minutes by default). It moves in jumps, a segment at a time.
steps.alt_code:
// 4. change retention.ms and nothing else
val op = AlterConfigOp(ConfigEntry("retention.ms", Duration.ofDays(3).toMillis().toString()),
    AlterConfigOp.OpType.SET)
val topic = ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.TOPIC, "settlement-events")
admin.incrementalAlterConfigs(mapOf(topic to listOf(op))).all().get()

lab.title: Model segments, retention and compaction, then check a real broker
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. 14 of 16 fail. The two that pass are in `RetentionOnBrokerTest` and need no code from you: they show a real Kafka 4.4 broker doing what your model is about to do. Offsets 0 to 249 are two hours old, retention is one hour, and the earliest offset stops at a segment boundary below 250.

In `SegmentedLog.kt`, write `append`: build the `Rec`, roll to a new `Segment(endOffset)` when the active segment already has records and this one would push it past `segmentBytes`, then add the record and move `endOffset` on.
Write `deleteExpired`: walk from the oldest segment, stop at the first one that hasn't expired, and remove the expired ones whole. If that removed every segment, add an empty one at `endOffset`.
Run the tests. `SegmentedLogTest` should pass.
In `Compaction.java`, write `compact`: one pass to find each key's last offset, and a second pass to copy the survivors in order, dropping tombstones older than `deleteRetentionMs`.
Run the tests until all 16 pass.
hints: Roll before you append: the size check uses the record you're about to add. A segment that is still empty takes any record, however big.
A segment has expired when `nowMs - maxTimestampMs > retentionMs`. An empty segment's `maxTimestampMs` is -1, so check `records.isNotEmpty()` first, or an empty segment looks ancient.

In Java, `Rec` is a Kotlin data class: call `r.getKey()`, `r.getValue()`, `r.getOffset()` and `r.getTimestampMs()`. A `HashMap<String, Long>` filled in offset order leaves each key mapped to its last offset.

drill.title: Write the retention sweep from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `deleteExpired(segments, nowMs, retentionMs)` for a list of segments, oldest first, where each segment has `records` and `maxTimestampMs`. Delete whole expired segments from the front, stop at the first one that hasn't expired, and return how many you deleted. Then compare with the answer. Did you stop at the first young segment, or did you skip over it?

recap: A topic is a set of partitions. Each partition is its own log with its own offsets, and order holds only inside one partition, so records that must stay in order share a key.

On disk, a partition is a directory of segment files named by base offset. Only the active segment takes new records; it rolls at `segment.bytes` (1 GiB) or `segment.ms` (7 days). Sparse `.index` and `.timeindex` files find an offset or a time without reading everything.

Retention deletes whole segments, oldest first, once a segment's newest record passes `retention.ms` or the partition is over `retention.bytes`. Records live at least that long, and the earliest offset jumps a segment at a time.

Compaction keeps at least the last record per key in closed segments. Offsets and order never change, and a tombstone (a null value) deletes a key, staying for `delete.retention.ms` so consumers see it.

Tiered storage (ready since Kafka 3.9) moves closed segments to object storage and keeps recent ones local. Diskless topics (KIP-1150, accepted, not shipped in 4.4) would write straight to object storage and stop brokers copying to each other, at the cost of slower writes.
The limit: each partition's newest records still live on one broker's disk. If that disk dies, they die with it. The next lesson keeps copies on other brokers.
closing:
We started with a café owner who threw out whole notebooks, and an inspector who found a twelve-day-old order. Kafka does the same: retention deletes whole segments, so records live at least as long as you asked, and often longer. Compaction keeps a different promise: the last value for every key.

Start the lab broker again, write a few records, and list `/var/lib/kafka/data/` inside it. Count the `.log` files in a partition's directory, then run `kafka-get-offsets.sh --time earliest` and match the number to a file name.

Next, we'll keep copies of each partition on three brokers, and ask when a new record counts as safe.

quiz.q: A topic has `retention.ms` of 7 days and the default 1 GiB `segment.bytes`, but it receives only a few megabytes a day. How long can its oldest records stay readable?
options: Exactly 7 days
7 days, plus up to 5 minutes for the next retention check
Up to about 14 days: the segment rolls on `segment.ms` after 7 days, then waits until its newest record is 7 days old
Forever, because a segment under 1 GiB never rolls
quiz.why: The segment never fills 1 GiB, so it rolls on time, after `segment.ms` (7 days). Its newest record is then almost 7 days younger than its oldest, and the file goes only when that newest record passes 7 days. The last option forgets `segment.ms`; the first two forget that retention works on whole files.

quiz.q: A consumer group was stopped for 9 days on a topic that keeps 7. When it starts again, its committed offset points into a deleted segment. The consumer uses the default settings. What happens?
options: It fails to start with an OffsetOutOfRangeException
It carries on from the earliest offset still on disk
The broker brings the deleted segment back from a copy
It jumps to the end of the partition and skips everything in between, without an error
quiz.why: When the committed offset no longer exists, `auto.offset.reset` decides, and its default is `latest`. The consumer moves to the end, and the records in between are skipped with no error. `earliest` would give the second option and `none` the first. Every copy of the partition deletes the same segments, so there's nothing to bring back.

quiz.q: A compacted topic `card-status` has these records in closed segments: offset 10 card-7=active, 11 card-8=active, 12 card-7=frozen, 13 card-7=null. The cleaner runs, well within `delete.retention.ms`. What can a consumer read from these offsets afterwards?
options: 11 card-8=active and 13 card-7=null
11 card-8=active and 12 card-7=frozen
11 card-8=active only
All four records, renumbered as offsets 0 to 3
quiz.why: Only the last record per key survives: 11 for card-8, and 13, the tombstone, for card-7. The tombstone stays for `delete.retention.ms` so that consumers learn about the delete; the third option is what you get after that window. Offsets never change.

quiz.q: The `payments` topic must keep 13 months, and the cloud bill shows a lot of traffic between brokers in different zones. On Kafka 4.4, what does turning on tiered storage change?
options: It stops brokers copying data to each other, because the object store now holds the copies
It moves the active segment to the object store too, so brokers need almost no disk
Old closed segments move to the object store, which saves broker disk; copying between brokers, and its cross-zone traffic, stay as they were
Nothing, until you also set `cleanup.policy=tiered`
quiz.why: Tiered storage only moves closed segments older than `local.retention.*`. Writing is unchanged: every batch is still copied to two other brokers. Removing that traffic is what diskless topics (KIP-1150) aim at, and they're accepted but not in Kafka 4.4. The active segment always stays local, and the switch is `remote.storage.enable=true`, not a cleanup policy.

quiz.q: From The log: Kafka's one big idea: an audit job calls `assign`, then `seek(tp, 50)`, on a partition whose earliest offset is now 104 after retention. The consumer has `auto.offset.reset=none`. What happens?
options: `seek` throws at once, because offset 50 is gone
`seek` succeeds, and the next `poll` throws OffsetOutOfRangeException
The next `poll` starts at 104 without a word
The next `poll` returns offsets 50 to 103 from another copy
quiz.why: `seek` only sets a number inside the consumer, so it can't fail on a missing offset. The fetch for offset 50 fails on the broker, and with `auto.offset.reset=none` the consumer throws `OffsetOutOfRangeException` from `poll`. The lab's broker test checks exactly this. With `earliest`, it would quietly start at 104 instead.

flashcards.back: One file of a partition's log, named after its first (base) offset, such as `00000000000000000208.log`. Only the newest, the active segment, takes new records.
When the next batch would push it past `segment.bytes` (1 GiB by default), or when it's older than `segment.ms` (7 days) as a new record arrives.

flashcards.front: Which record does age-based retention look at to decide whether a segment goes?
flashcards.back: The segment's newest record. The whole file is deleted once that record is older than `retention.ms`.

flashcards.front: With tiered storage on, which segments stay on the broker's disk?
flashcards.back: The active segment and the recent closed ones, as set by `local.retention.ms` and `local.retention.bytes`. Older closed segments live in object storage, and `retention.ms` still decides when data is deleted everywhere.
A record with a key and a null value. On a compacted topic it deletes the key, and it stays for `delete.retention.ms` (1 day by default) after the cleaner first reaches it.

flashcards.front: Does compaction change offsets or order?
flashcards.back: No. Survivors keep their offsets and their order, so a compacted partition has gaps.

flashcards.front: What is the smallest `segment.bytes` in Kafka 4.x?
flashcards.back: 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes). Kafka 4.0 raised it from 14 bytes.

terms.plain: One of the logs a topic is split into, each with its own offsets. Records with the same key land in the same partition.
One file of a partition's log, plus its index files, named after the offset of its first record.
The newest segment of a partition, the only one that takes new records. Compaction never touches it.
Deleting old data by age (`retention.ms`) or size (`retention.bytes`), a whole segment at a time.
The oldest offset a partition still holds, also called the log start offset. Retention moves it forward in jumps.
Cleaning a partition so that at least the last record for every key remains, with offsets unchanged.
A record with a key and a null value: on a compacted topic, the way to delete a key.
Keeping recent segments on the broker's disk and older closed segments in object storage, a cheap file store in the cloud.

explain_back.prompt: A friend set `retention.ms` to one hour on a test topic and is surprised that records written three hours ago are still readable. Explain why, and what they could change to see retention act sooner.
explain_back.answer: Retention deletes whole segment files, and a segment goes only when its newest record is older than `retention.ms`. On a quiet test topic, the active segment keeps taking records for a long time, because the defaults are 1 GiB and 7 days per segment, so the three-hour-old records share a file with newer ones. The broker also only checks every `log.retention.check.interval.ms`, 5 minutes by default. To see retention sooner, make the segments roll sooner: lower `segment.ms` on the test topic, or `segment.bytes` (1 MiB at least). Then old records end up in closed segments that can expire on their own.

deeper.body:
**How the diskless designs differ.** WarpStream's agents keep nothing of their own: they speak the Kafka protocol, keep all data in object storage and keep their bookkeeping in a service WarpStream runs. Its docs say 99 in 100 writes finish within about 500 ms on standard S3 (the 99th percentile, or p99), and within about 170 ms on S3 Express One Zone, a faster kind of S3. AutoMQ, a fork of Kafka under the Apache license, replaces local segments with a write-ahead log in front of object storage. Aiven's open fork Inkless is the testbed for KIP-1150 itself. These are the makers' own figures, so measure at the guarantees you need before you compare them with a classic cluster's few milliseconds.

**Tiered storage keeps improving.** Kafka 4.3 and 4.4 added refinements, such as letting a new copy of a partition start from the last offset already in object storage, instead of copying everything from another broker, and delaying uploads (`remote.copy.lag.ms`).

**Compaction settings worth knowing.** `min.compaction.lag.ms` keeps recent values uncompacted for a while, so consumers see them. `max.compaction.lag.ms` asks the cleaner to compact a record within some time, though the design doc calls it a deadline the cleaner may miss. Its default is `Long.MAX`, which means a value replaced or deleted by a tombstone has no deadline for leaving the disk unless you set one. And `kafka-log-dirs.sh --describe` shows how much disk each partition uses on each broker, the quickest way to find the partition that retention isn't keeping in check.
